endorsements.quote: Once intake is completed, the system can generate a draft summary for review, but no patient-facing conclusions should be issued without clinician approval.
In practical terms, triage should be reviewed by a named clinician or appropriately trained team member before appointment allocation or major pathway decisions are made.
These design features make the tension visible and correctable within the workflow rather than relying on clinician vigilance alone.

At minimum, a pre-agreed escalation protocol should specify: (a) the named clinical role responsible for review (e.g., duty gastroenterologist, clinical nurse specialist, or on-call liaison psychiatry); (b) a maximum review window (e.g., within 4 hours during working hours, or a defined out-of-hours pathway); (c) the clinical channel through which escalation occurs (e.g., direct notification to the electronic health record task list with audit trail, or direct phone contact for imminent risk); and (d) a documented fallback procedure when the primary reviewer is unavailable, including escalation to the next designated role.
For that reason, implementation should be phased.

Because the task can be narrowly defined around alarm features, symptom pattern, psychosocial complexity, and routing urgency, it is also more governable than open-ended diagnostic AI, as Bedi et al. ( 11 ) and the World Health Organization ( 12 ) would support.

Paper, telephone, or assisted completion routes are needed for patients with limited digital access, language barriers, low health literacy, or symptom severity that makes extensive questionnaires difficult.

Responsible implementation therefore requires periodic fairness audits that assess not only model outputs but downstream decisions such as urgency assignment, referral to psychology, investigation patterns, and patient-reported experience.

Fourth, escalation-sensitive content—suicidal ideation, self-harm, severe nutritional risk—should bypass the generative synthesis step entirely and follow deterministic, rule-based routing, as LLM-generated paraphrases of safety-critical disclosures introduce unacceptable risk.

unlisted_practices: Collect only the minimum clinically justified data needed for pre-consultation triage (data minimization).
Obtain informed consent in plain language covering data collected, AI summary generation, storage, access, and sharing, with opt-out for de-identified data use that does not affect care.

Treat AI-generated summaries as part of the clinical record subject to the same retention, correction, access, privacy and security policies, including encryption, role-based access control, and audit logging.
Complete a data protection impact assessment before deploying any system that collects mental health disclosures.
Do not collect high-risk mental health information through automated intake unless the service can commit to a named reviewer, review window, clinical channel, and fallback procedure.
Preserve provenance and keep original patient text visible to clinicians alongside AI summaries, indicating source of each statement and uncertainty.
Constrain psychosocial summarization to extractive or template-bound output with each claim anchored to a patient-reported statement.
Display original patient text before the summary for clinically salient psychosocial content and require clinician acknowledgment before routing.
Flag low-confidence psychosocial attributions with a visible mismatch flag prompting review of the original text.
Do not treat missingness, brevity, or linguistic difference in patient responses as low complexity.
Audit false reassurance events and separate alarm-feature handling from psychosocial profiling.
Evaluate in phases (feasibility, operational outcomes, patient benefit) with predefined outcome measures and equity audits across subgroups.
Train clinicians in using AI pre-consultation summaries appropriately.
Do not allow autonomous scheduling or referral without human confirmation.
Do not use AI triage output to recommend interventions the service cannot deliver.
Use AI intake to supplement rather than replace validated screening instruments and ingest their scores as structured inputs.
Do not make patient completion of AI intake mandatory when barriers exist.
Avoid mandatory audio or video capture in routine care.
Refine tools through iterative clinician feedback and make clinician correction of summaries straightforward.
Include in the intake a clear statement that the tool does not provide diagnosis or emergency advice.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/proposal paper outlining essential conditions, safeguards, and frameworks for deploying generative AI for pre-consultation triage in DGBI, without presenting original empirical data.
